items.title: mori 森
items.text:
memento mori: every tree dies; your work doesn't.

mori tends a forest of git and jj worktrees for you and your coding agents. It keeps one clone per repo in a fixed layout, gives every tree an owner and a lifetime, moves work between agents, and cleans up without ever losing a change.

Website: https://nevzheng.github.io/mori/

Status: pre-alpha. The API is mori.v1alpha1 and the binary is 0.x: there are no stability guarantees, and anything may change in any release. Nothing useful works yet.

items.title: Build
items.text:
Bazel is the build system. cargo works too, but Bazel is the supported path.

bazel test //...            # build everything, run clippy and rustfmt, run the tests
bazel run //crates/cli:mori -- --version

items.title: License
items.text:
Apache-2.0.

More to come

mori is young. Guides, a command reference and design notes will appear here as it grows.

items.title: Brand
items.text: How mori looks and sounds. Use this for the website, the README, the CLI's messages and anything else that speaks for the project.

items.title: Name
items.text:
• mori, always lowercase, including at the start of a sentence.
  • It comes from 森 (mori), Japanese for forest. The character is three 木 (tree): one above, two below. mori tends a forest of worktrees.
  • Show 森 in a proper font. Don't hand-draw it or imitate brush lettering.

items.title: Tagline
items.text:
memento mori: every tree dies; your work doesn't.

Trees come and go; mori makes sure the work in them is never lost.

items.title: Voice
items.text:
• Plain. Short sentences, everyday words. Say what happens, not how impressive it is.
  • Calm. mori deals with people's work; it never sounds alarmed or flippant about it.
  • A little wry, where it helps. Never at the reader's expense.
  • Honest. mori is a hobby project and pre-alpha, and says so.

items.title: Values
items.text:
• Never lose work.
  • A high bar: great engineering, product and UX.
  • No slop.

items.title: Logo
items.text:
Three pines arranged like 森: one above, two below.

  • Files: docs/assets/logo.svg. It works at every size down to a 16 px favicon.
  • Colours: the two forest greens below. Don't recolour, outline, rotate, stretch or add effects.
  • Space: leave at least a quarter of the logo's width clear around it.
  • Lockup: the logo followed by the name mori in the body font.

items.title: Colours
items.text:
Based on Everforest (MIT), adjusted so every text colour passes WCAG AA (a contrast of at least 4.5:1). The site follows the reader's light or dark setting.

Role Light Dark Use Background #FDF6E3 #2D353B Page Surface #F4F0D9 #343F44 Code blocks, raised panels Text #5C6A72 #D3C6AA Body copy Primary #4F6B2A #A7C080 Buttons, highlights Accent #5C6F00 #83C092 Hover and focus Links #2F6F8F #7FBBB3 Links Logo top #8DA101 #8DA101 The upper pine Logo base #35A77C #35A77C The two lower pines

items.title: Type
items.text: The site's default sans-serif for text, and its monospace for code and commands. No display or novelty fonts.

items.title: Using Japanese respectfully
items.text:
• Use 森 for what it means, forest, and say so plainly.
  • No stereotyped "Japanese" styling: no imitation-Asian fonts, torii gates, cherry blossoms, samurai or zen clichés. The forest carries the identity.
  • 森 is also a common Japanese family name. Don't write copy that treats mori as a person.
  • Have a native speaker review any new Japanese text before it ships.

items.title: Contributing to mori
items.text: Thanks for your interest. mori is a hobby project: I build it in my free time, for fun. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

items.title: Expectations
items.text: I reply when I can, and sometimes not at all. There's no schedule, roadmap promise or support guarantee. A quiet issue isn't a rejection, and a closed one isn't personal. mori is pre-alpha: anything may change in any release.

items.title: Ways to help
items.text:
• Report a bug: use the bug form. Include your version (mori --version), OS, the command, what you expected and what happened.
  • Suggest a feature: use the feature form and start with the problem, not the solution.
  • Ask a question: use the question form.
  • Fix something small (typos, docs, an obvious bug): open a PR directly.
  • Build something bigger: see Spec- and design-driven development below. Unsure whether it fits? Open an issue and ask first.
  • Security issues: never in a public issue. See SECURITY.md.

items.title: The bar
items.text:
mori aims for great engineering, product and UX, and holds every change to a high engineering standard. For a good picture of what that looks like, Google's Engineering Practices are an excellent reference, especially:

  • The standard of code review
  • What to look for in a code review
  • Small CLs
  • Writing good CL descriptions

Use whatever tools help. Coding agents are welcome, and we encourage using them responsibly. If AI helped, you're welcome to say so in a PR comment. (Not in the description: it becomes the commit message.)

Slop isn't accepted: changes the author doesn't understand, can't explain, or didn't verify. Every contribution meets the same bar, however it was made:

  • You own it. You understand every line, can say why it's right, and answer review questions yourself.
  • It's verified. Tests prove the behavior; user-visible behavior starts as a spec scenario. bazel test //... passes.
  • It's one CL. One small, focused change per pull request.
  • It comes with its design. Changes beyond a small fix include their design doc, written first.

items.title: Spec- and design-driven development
items.text:
We write the spec and the design first, then the code. For a user-visible change, that means a Gherkin scenario in spec/cuj/ before the implementation. For new commands, new concepts, changes to the model or the API, and anything hard to undo, it also means a design doc in docs/design/<area>/, following Apache Spark's SPIP format:

  • Q1–Q8, with no jargon: what you're trying to do, what it doesn't solve, how it's done today, what's new, who cares, the risks, how long it takes, and how we'll know it worked.
  • Appendices: A. API (proto) changes · B. Design sketch · C. Rejected designs · D. Failure modes and security · E. Test plan (CUJs and scenarios) · F. Migration.

The doc is part of the change, and either order works:

  • Doc first: send the design doc on its own for early feedback on the direction, then the code in follow-up PRs.
  • Doc and code together: send them in the same PR.

Either way, reviews start with the doc. Unsure whether something needs one? Open an issue and ask.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
• Bazel is the build system: bazel test //... builds everything, runs clippy and rustfmt on every target, and runs the tests, including the end-to-end CUJ scenarios.
  • cargo works too, but Bazel is the supported path.
  • The API is proto-first: edit proto/, run bazel run //tools/protogen, commit the result.
  • AGENTS.md has the full working rules; they apply to humans and agents alike.

items.title: Pull requests
items.text:
• One CL per PR, squash-merged: the PR title and description become the commit.
  • Title: a Conventional Commit, <type>(<scope>)!: <subject> (CI checks it).
  • Description: what changed and why (see Google's guide above). No attribution lines (Co-Authored-By, "Generated with"); CI rejects them.
  • CI must pass. Draft PRs are fine for early feedback.
  • Stale PRs: if a PR waits on its author for a few weeks, I may close it; reopen any time.

items.title: Reviews
items.text: Reviews use Conventional Comments (issue:, suggestion:, nitpick:, question:, …) and are about the change, never the person.

items.title: Code of conduct
items.text: Everyone taking part in mori follows the code of conduct.

items.title: License
items.text: Unless you say otherwise, anything you submit is licensed under Apache-2.0, like the rest of mori (section 5 of the license). No CLA.

items.title: Design docs
items.text:
mori is built spec- and design-first. New commands, new concepts, changes to the model or the API, and anything hard to undo come with a design doc. Small fixes don't need one; if you're unsure, open an issue and ask.

Docs follow Apache Spark's SPIP format: eight plain-language questions, then appendices for the details. Start from TEMPLATE.md.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
docs/design/
  README.md
  TEMPLATE.md
  <area>/
    <what-it-does>.md              a doc on its own
    <what-it-does>/README.md       a doc with diagrams or large appendices, beside it
  • Area: a crate or subsystem, such as cli, core, api or store. Add a new directory when none fits.
  • Name: plain English saying what the design does, in lowercase words joined by hyphens, e.g. cli/init-sets-up-the-root.md or core/cleanup-never-loses-work.md. No numbers in names.
  • Numbers live inside the doc: its metadata table links the tracking issue and the PR, which gives each design a stable reference without clashes.

items.title: Statuses
items.text:
Only accepted designs live on main. Drafts and reviews happen in pull requests, and a design that isn't accepted is closed with its PR: the discussion stays there.

Status Where Meaning draft an open PR Being written. Feedback welcome, nothing decided. review an open PR Ready for review. accepted main Agreed. Code lands against it. superseded main Replaced by a later design; the doc links to it.

An accepted doc isn't rewritten when plans change: fix small errors in place, and write a new doc that supersedes it for a real change of direction.

items.title: How a doc moves
items.text:
The doc is part of the change, not a gate. Either order works:

  • Doc first: send the doc on its own PR for early feedback on the direction, then the code in follow-up PRs.
  • Doc and code together: send them in the same PR.

Either way, review starts with the doc. The status changes in the same PR that settles it. A design issue (the "Design proposal" form) is optional, useful for testing an idea before writing.

items.title: Title: what this design does, in plain English
items.text: Author @github-handle Status draft  Area cli  Issue #123  PR #124  Created YYYY-MM-DD Updated YYYY-MM-DD

items.title: Q1. What are you trying to do?
Q2. What problems is this not trying to solve?
Q3. How is it done today, and what are the limits?
Q4. What is new in your approach, and why will it work?
Q5. Who cares? If it works, what difference does it make?
Q7. How long will it take?
Q8. How will we know it worked?
Appendix D. Failure modes and security
Appendix E. Test plan
items.text:
Scenario: <the behavior, in the user's words>
  Given <a starting state>
  When I run "mori <command>"
  Then <what the user sees>
